error_description: When presented with a 3D orthogonal coordinate system drawn on a 2D surface, students may interpret the oblique axis as a negative direction on a standard 2D Cartesian plane.
example: Looking at a 3D sketch, Vera interpreted the third axis drawn diagonally down-and-left as indicating a negative value, stating 'it means that this one is negative. He should have drawn it this way'.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: In identifying the basic repeating unit of a semiregular tessellation, students may incorrectly select a single regular polygon instead of the necessary combination of shapes that tile the plane.
example: For a tessellation made of hexagons and triangles, a student circled a single hexagon as the basic repeating tile.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education. Monograph

error_description: Teachers accept empirical evidence, such as testing a few specific cases or using a visual demonstration, as a mathematically valid formal proof.
example: Five teachers rated an empirically based argument, which tore up the angles of a triangle to form a straight line, as a valid proof.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: When finding the equation of a circle passing through three given points, a student inappropriately sets up an analytic system using only two of the points, resulting in an unresolvable equation in two variables.
example: Setting up (7 - h)^2 + (0 - k)^2 = r^2 and (5 - h)^2 + (4 - k)^2 = r^2 and solving to get 2k = h - 2.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: The prospective teacher lacks conceptual knowledge of geometric formulas, such as the derivation of pi, and instead relies on rote memory aids and arbitrary rules to teach students.
example: Think about it. Area has an r sound in it. A-r-e-a and radius.
authors: Margaret Eisenhart, Hilda Borko, Robert Underhill, Catherine Brown, Doug Jones and Patricia Agard
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students draw a figure but fail to recognize its necessary properties, such as assuming a right triangle does not have to have a longest side or a largest angle.
example: Even though they drew a right triangle, 12 students did not think that such a triangle had to have a longest side and 7 students did not think it required a largest angle.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students answer generalized class inclusion and relationship questions by drawing specific figures and deriving answers from the visual appearance of their own drawings.
example: Given that triangles ABC and DEF were similar or congruent, students drew specific figures and answered whether certain angles or sides were equal depending on their own diagram.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Pupils hold the conception that the sum of the angles of a triangle depends on its shape and size, specifically believing that larger triangles have a larger sum of angles.
example: When asked to predict the sum of the angles of three contrasting triangles, pupils made predictions ranging from 160 degrees to 770 degrees.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students attempt to prove the general triangle inequality conjecture by inappropriately citing the Pythagorean theorem formula and using static rather than transformational reasoning.
example: A participant stated that Mary's conjecture is true 'because if you look at the formula a squared plus b squared equals c squared' and formed a nondynamic triangle with her hands.
authors: Caroline (Caro) Williams-Pierce, Elizabeth L. Pier, Candace Walkington, Rebecca Boncoddo, Virginia Clinton, Martha W. Alibali and Mitchell J. Nathan
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: When equipartitioning a single whole, students fail to apply necessary criteria such as creating equal-sized pieces, obtaining the correct number of shares, and exhausting the whole.
example: Students drew 6 parallel lines on a rectangle to share for 6 people, resulting in 7 parts, or removed equal-sized pieces without using the entire whole because 'at home four children would never be allowed to eat an entire cake'.

error_description: Young students hold the initially productive belief that fair shares of a single whole must have the exact same size and shape, failing to recognize that equal parts need not be congruent.
example: When children encounter two identical rectangles—one split in half vertically and the other split in half diagonally—they may struggle to recognize the pieces are equal in size because they lack the same shape.
authors: Jere Confrey, Alan P. Maloney, Andrew K. Corley

error_description: Students struggle to recognize a sector as a specific proportion of a circle, such as a quarter, if it is presented in an atypical orientation rather than with standard horizontal and vertical radii.
example: A student found the task difficult because the 'clothes' sector was not oriented as an 'outright quarter' with vertical and horizontal boundary lines.

error_description: Teachers hold an exclusive, partitional concept image of quadrilaterals rather than an inclusive, hierarchical one, preventing them from recognizing subset relationships among shapes.
example: When asked if it was possible for a parallelogram to have congruent diagonals, teachers answered incorrectly because their concept image of a parallelogram excluded rectangles as a special type.

error_description: Children restrict their definition of a triangle to a prototypical isosceles or equilateral shape with a horizontal base, failing to recognize right-angled or non-prototypical triangles as valid triangles.
example: When shown a right-angled triangle, some students called it a 'half-triangle, because if you put two of them together you get a real triangle.'
authors: Doug Clarke, Barbara Clarke, Anne Roche

error_description: Students empirically derive an incomplete formula by only testing examples within a limited example space, missing edge cases where variables share common divisors.
example: Concluding that the number of squares crossed by a diagonal in an n by k rectangle is always n + k - 1, which only holds true when n and k are relatively prime.
grade_band_as_declared: middle school to preservice elementary school teachers
authors: Rina Zazkis, Peter Liljedahl, Egan J. Chernoff

error_description: Students hold conflicting ontological views on parallel lines, with one viewing them as idealized theoretical constructs that never meet, and another viewing them as physical drawings that will eventually intersect.
example: One student argues parallel lines cannot intersect, while another extends the lines drawn on their paper to show a meeting point very far away.
mathematical_topic: parallel lines and linear equation systems

error_description: Students inappropriately applied general geometry terms like 'feet' or 'length' to describe the turtle's path, rather than using the turtle-specific intrinsic measure of discrete 'steps'.
example: Edna suggested "Step forward two feet" and Luke asked "Do you know length?"
grade_band_as_declared: middle and high school students between grades 8 and 10

error_description: In a dynamic physical situation (a pendulum swing), the student conceptualized an angle as having only one side or ray, failing to identify the second reference line that forms the angle.
example: When explaining the pendulum effect of falling, she described it as 'The angle from the wall where the rope is fastened and to me,' and used her hand to indicate only a single line.

error_description: Students lack the 'projection' mental process, failing to project points from the unit circle onto the axes to geometrically interpret trigonometric values, instead relying on partially memorized, disjointed rules.
example: When trying to find the inverse sine of -0.974927912, Diana correctly located the point for 10π/7 on the circle but failed to project it onto the y-axis to relate the values, instead attempting to apply a memorized rule about adding a negative sign.

error_description: A student incorrectly believed he could not draw a parallelogram using a generalized rectangle procedure because the shape's lines were "slanted," failing to conceptually link the visual slant to the intrinsic geometric properties and angles defined in the Logo code.
example: When trying to draw a parallelogram, Jonathan said, 'Because the lines are slanted... This thing ain't slanted. It looks slanted, but if you put it back it wouldn't be slanted. Anyway you move this, it wouldn't be a rectangle.'

error_description: Students persistently confused the angle of turn (the exterior angle executed by the turtle) with the constructed interior angle of a polygon in turtle geometry.
Students believed that the steepness of a straight hill or ramp was not constant but continually increased as one moved higher up the incline.
example: When looking at a drawing of a hill, Terry claimed it was steeper at the top ''Cause it's like higher up on the angle.'

error_description: The student believed there was a static relationship between the endpoints of the vector and the vertices of the pre-image and image, assuming that if the vector's tail moved, the pre-image would move with it.
example: The pre-image and its relationship to E was static. That is, wherever E would move, that (pre-image) would follow.

error_description: The student initially believed that a zero vector meant no translation occurred, as a vector with zero magnitude conflicted with his motion-based conception of a translation.
example: He was thinking that a vector has two points and if the magnitude of the vector was zero, there wouldn't be a vector at all, so the pre-image would not move.

error_description: Students incorrectly believed that a parallelogram is a type of rectangle, incorrectly manipulating the angles of their dynamic figural concept of a rectangle to produce a parallelogram rather than recognizing class inclusion in the other direction.
example: Some children responded that 'they are both rectangles' when comparing the rectangle and parallelogram.
authors: Crystal Walcott, Doris Mohr, Signe E. Kastberg

error_description: Students exhibited an atomistic perception that blocked their understanding of 'small infinity' in continuous geometric contexts, believing that a process of inward contraction or division must eventually stop due to lack of physical space.
example: When asked to continue a spiral drawing inwards, Stefan (grade 4) stopped and claimed 'Here there is no room to continue!' and insisted that no matter how thin the pencil, it would not be possible to continue.

error_description: Students' geometric reasoning is inflexible; their ability to find the area of a shape is heavily dependent on its visual orientation and the absence of superfluous information.
example: Finding the area of a right-angled triangle in a standard orientation yielded an 88% success rate, but the same triangle rotated yielded a 64% success rate.
authors: Adolf af Ekenstam and Margita Nilsson

error_description: Children hold a spontaneous, phenomenological concept of a circle relying merely on visually salient attributes like roundness and symmetry, failing to define it by its formal geometric properties.
example: Alex states a genuine circle must be 'quite rotund' with a 'roundabout line with no ripples' and 'smoothly round.'

error_description: Using physical templates leads children to believe that mathematical circles are concrete, objective entities that only exist if there is a corresponding physical tool or pattern available.
example: When unable to find a template exactly double the size, children claim 'such a circle is rather rare' or 'a circle in such a size does not exist.'

error_description: Learners refuse to recognize a valid geometric shape if it is presented in a non-standard orientation, confusing its defining properties with its specific spatial alignment.
example: Children will refuse to consider a specific figure to be a right-angled triangle because of its orientation.

error_description: Students exhibit geometrical rigidity where their conceptions become trapped by a diagram, leaving them unable to perceive a line or component in an alternative role.
example: A student is unable to use the line AD as a 'side' of a sub-triangle because they only perceive it as the 'height' of the larger triangle ABC.

error_description: When unable to generate an appropriate visual schema or conceptualize the spatial mathematical structure, students resort to superficial and inappropriate calculations combining the isolated numbers present in the problem text.
example: A student attempts to solve the painted cube problem by simply dividing 27 (the number of small cubes) by 4 (the four different types of painted cubes) because they are 'just looking at the numbers'.
authors: K. JENNIFER CAMPBELL, KEVIN F. COLLIS AND JANE M. WATSON

error_description: Students inappropriately rephrase given disjunctions by substituting semantic relationships between properties, which can inadvertently change the logical meaning or render the statement a tautology.
example: A student substitutes the property 'is not acute' with 'is obtuse', or replaces 'is equilateral' based on the warrant that 'equilateral triangles are acute', leading them to incorrectly rephrase a geometric disjunction.
authors: Paul Christian Dawkins & John Paul Cook

error_description: Children perceive the continuous variation of an area during deformation in a discontinuous manner, believing the area remains constant until it nears an extreme limit.
example: When tilting a parallelogram, students initially think the area does not change, but then suddenly perceive it as becoming very small only when it is close to being completely flattened.
grade_band_as_declared: CM1 (9-10 ans) et un CM2 (10-11 ans)

error_description: Students struggle to draw three-dimensional objects on a two-dimensional surface without distortion because they attempt to preserve all characteristic properties, such as 90-degree angles and parallel lines.
example: Jeroen made many attempts to draw a cube... 'It's just not a cube, is it?', he sighed. It is, of course, impossible to make a two-dimensional drawing of a spatial object such as a cube, leaving all its properties intact.
grade_band_as_declared: 12 to 16 year olds (seventh and eighth graders)

error_description: Students confuse the definitions and visual properties of parallelograms and trapezoids.
example: When asked to place a point D to complete a parallelogram ABCD, some students drew a trapezoid instead.

error_description: Students intuitively assume that two shapes with visually different contours cannot have equivalent areas, even when they can be proven equal by translation.
example: When asked to prove that two areas formed between parallel curves are equivalent, students intuitively react that the two areas are not equal and that 'there is nothing to prove'.

error_description: Students hold the intuitive notion that area equivalence coincides with congruence, believing that non-congruent figures cannot have equal areas.
example: A student states, "there is no possibility for having the same area, because there is no symmetry" or "to be sure I had to know whether these triangles are congruent, which does not hold, so they are different [in area]."
authors: George Kospentaris & Panagiotis Spyrou & Dionyssios Lappas

error_description: Students erroneously assume that the area of a shape remains constant if one dimension or side increases by the exact same additive amount that another decreases.
example: A student believes a triangle with sides 1 and 9 has the same area as one with sides 3 and 7, explaining, "You subtract an amount from one side and you add it on the other, in order to balance it..."
authors: George Kospentaris & Panagiotis Spyrou & Dionyssios Lappas

error_description: Students incorrectly believe that horizontal objects must have horizontal images and vertical objects must have vertical images, or vice versa, under geometric reflection.
grade_band_as_declared: secondary school class aged 11 and 12 years; 13-14 years old

error_description: Students mistakenly view reflection as moving a physical mirror along a line rather than as a mathematical folding operation, leading them to believe there can be multiple correct images.
example: Pupils justified their conclusion that there could be more than one correct image by showing how the mirror could be moved—still standing on the same line—to produce a movement of the image.
grade_band_as_declared: secondary school class aged 11 and 12 years; 13-14 years old

error_description: Students are unable to spontaneously see or discriminate the mathematically relevant subfigures within a complex geometric figure due to competing visual and gestalt factors that screen out necessary elements.
example: When shown a circle tangent to a rectangle and asked to find the length of a segment, students fail to recognize the segments as radii because the visually dominant subfigures obscure the mathematically useful ones.

error_description: Students apply finite physical reality to geometric infinity.
example: Number of points on a segment corresponds to its length; cannot draw point for smallest triangle.
mathematical_subtopic: infinitely close and infinitely many points
authors: Vida Manfreda Kolar, Tatjana Hodnik Cadez

error_description: Students use geometric characteristics (length) to determine numerosity of infinite point sets, ignoring 1-1 correspondence.
example: CD has more points than AB because CD is longer, despite acknowledging correspondence.
authors: LUIS E. MORENO A. AND GUILLERMINA WALDEGG

error_description: Students intuitively treat rotation globally as a movement, struggling to interpret it as a standard angle defined by two intersecting lines (e.g., an initial and final position).
example: When asked to represent the rotation of a wheel or door, many students accurately matched the size of the rotation but used only one arm of a bent straw or could not identify the two lines making up the standard angle.
authors: MICHAEL C. MITCHELMORE and PAUL WHITE

error_description: Students confuse geometrically distinct entities, such as a segment and its length, relying on uncontrolled associations without applying a conceptual control mechanism.
example: When asked 'What is the distance between two points?', a student answers 'A segment', and even after the teacher corrects them by saying 'it is the length of the segment', the student insists 'But this is exactly what I have said.'
grade_band_as_declared: multiple grades including primary, high school, and college

error_description: Students appear to lack understanding of spatial concepts like 'middle' or 'flat', leading to potential misdiagnoses of learning difficulties, because these abstract terms do not exist in their home language.
example: A student was unable to point to the object in the 'middle' of a row during an assessment, but successfully completed the task after the concept was explained through concrete experiences.

error_description: Students incorrectly assume that uniformly scaling the linear dimensions of a two-dimensional shape results in an area scaled by the same linear factor, rather than the square of that factor.
example: Believing that an insect diagram with both length and width doubled will only have twice the area of the original, rather than four times the area.
authors: Annette Hilton & Geoff Hilton & Shelley Dole & Merrilyn Goos

error_description: Preservice teachers struggle to accurately sketch a mirror image or complete a symmetrical figure when the given line of symmetry is oblique, often distorting the image to create a congruent but non-symmetrical part.
example: When given an oblique line and half a figure, students distorted the mirror image, drawing a completed shape that was congruent but not actually symmetrical with respect to the oblique line.
authors: Roza Leikin & Abraham Berman & Orit Zaslavsky

error_description: Students rely on Euclidean intuition and the visual appearance of diagrams rather than formal axioms when determining geometric relationships, such as claiming disjoint lines intersect.
example: Claiming that lines AC and BD in a 4-point geometry are not parallel because they cross visually, ignoring that their set intersection is empty.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Teachers mistakenly believe that the diagonals of a non-square rectangle represent lines of symmetry.
example: Drawing the diagonals of a given rectangle in addition to, or instead of, the correct lines of symmetry.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Students inappropriately apply concepts and axioms from Euclidean geometry to spherical geometry, failing to incorporate the sphere's center or antipodal points when defining or drawing a spherical line.
example: When asked to draw a spherical line that passes through two points, a student draws an arbitrary arc connecting the points on the surface rather than a great circle that intersects the center of the sphere.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Students separate geometric images from conceptual constraints, relying on visual prototypes to mistakenly assume triangles must always be equilateral or have a horizontal base.
example: Describing a triangle by stating 'It is a geometric figure with three equal sides' or 'Draw a horizontal segment and then like two diagonals.'
authors: Nuria Joglar Prieto, Jose Maria Sordo Juanena & Jon R. Star
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Students assume every quadrilateral is a parallelogram or erroneously believe the rhombus is the only parallelogram without right angles.
example: Drawing a parallelogram when asked to draw a general quadrilateral, or asking 'Isn't every quadrilateral a parallelogram?'
authors: Nuria Joglar Prieto, Jose Maria Sordo Juanena & Jon R. Star
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Students and teachers mistakenly accept that static diagrams or shapes formed by a finite rearrangement of circle wedges constitute an exact parallelogram, ignoring the necessary dynamic infinite limiting process.
example: Assuming it is acceptable to measure the area of the shape made by arranging 4, 8, 10, or 12 wedges simply by using the exact area of a parallelogram formula.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Prospective teachers possess a 'position-dependent base' image, believing the base is strictly the part, section, or surface of the object that touches the ground or is at the bottom, disregarding its actual geometric properties.
example: Naming a square prism a 'rectangular prism' when it is placed with its rectangular face touching the desk.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Prospective teachers overgeneralize the two-dimensional base concept to three dimensions, leading to a 'side/edge-dependent base' image where they believe the base of a 3D object is an edge rather than a face.
example: Stating that the edges of a prism with equal length are its bases, or suggesting that any side where a height descends on a solid is a base.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Prospective teachers hold a 'naming-dependent base' image, where they do not define the base geometrically but rather rely solely on rote recall that the base is the part that gives the prism its name.
example: Explaining the base simply as 'the geometric figure which gives the prisms their names' without describing any geometric attributes of that base.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Students believe a proven geometric relationship becomes invalid when implicit diagrammatic suppositions are violated, treating the new configuration as a counterexample that refutes the statement.
example: Believing that the relationship PQ = DQ - BP is impossible when the intersecting line is drawn outside the square because segment BP becomes longer than segment DQ, making DQ - BP negative.
authors: Kotaro Komatsu, Yosuke Tsujiyama & Aruta Sakamaki
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Students mathematically model a three-dimensional solid based on one- or two-dimensional conceptions, focusing incorrectly on the scaling of edges or faces rather than the scaling of volume.
example: Grams per side: 0.4. Since 4 cm is twice as big as the other one, the weight will be twice as big and that is in accordance with grams per side 0.8 g.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Teachers may incorrectly classify verbally described loci of points by jumping to conclusions based on isolated 'key words' (e.g., 'ratio') without paying attention to the specific generating elements and their spatial relationships (e.g., whether a point lies on a given line).
example: A teacher identifies an item as a hyperbola solely by noting: 'For instance, here and here there are directrix, focus and ratio. So it is a hyperbola', incorrectly categorizing an ellipse. Another teacher later reflects, 'we missed that if the point is on the line the ratio is not important, it cannot be hyperbola or ellipse'.
authors: Boris Koichu, Orit Zaslavsky, Lea Dolev

error_description: A teacher imprecisely uses geometric terminology by referring to the wedge-shaped sectors of a circular spinner as squares.
example: "Everybody color in two more squares. Color in two more squares."

error_description: Students limit their definition of quadrilaterals to only squares and rectangles, failing to recognize that other four-sided figures with non-right angles are also quadrilaterals.
example: Students' definitions might simply say that quadrilaterals have four sides and four angles, limiting their definitions to only some quadrilaterals and excluding those with nonright angles.

error_description: A student uses slightly imprecise language to explain why a rectangle's area is larger than a parallelogram's when transformed, but still demonstrates a productive understanding of area conservation.
example: "Rectangle is bigger because we can transform the parallelogram to another rectangle. As such, the two rectangles have the same length but different width."

error_description: Students hold misconceptions about the concept of angles, defining them by their physical appearance like the width between sides rather than as a measure of rotation.
example: When asked to explain what an angle is, students responded with the width between two sides of the angle, the area formed by two sides, and the distance from the vertex to the label of the arrow.
journal: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education

error_description: Students have difficulty identifying subclass relationships among geometric shapes, struggling to accept that a shape can belong to a broader category.
example: Students believe that a square is not a rhombus.
journal: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education

error_description: Students incorrectly assume that non-corresponding opposite angles in a bow tie configuration in a circle are equal due to inappropriately generalizing properties of parallel lines.
example: Although the angles p-q and r-t are equal, students have a tendency to think that p-t and r-q are equal.
journal: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education

error_description: Students incorrectly conclude that the center of a circle tangent to two given lines is the midpoint of the line segment connecting the two tangent points.
example: many students later proposed in the same session that the center was the midpoint of the line that connects the tangent points.
journal: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education

error_description: Students erroneously assume that the distance between any two adjacent pins on a square grid is equal, regardless of whether they are orthogonally or diagonally adjacent.
example: Assuming a triangle with vertices at three adjacent dots forming a right angle is an isosceles triangle because the hypotenuse is 'one peg away' just like the legs.
grade_band_as_declared: first year of a two year Bachelor of Education degree programme
authors: Lyndon C. Martin and Jo Towers

error_description: Students identify and categorize geometric shapes based on their overall visual appearance rather than defining them by their mathematical properties.
example: A student refused to recognize a diamond shape as being a square simply because its sides were not oriented vertically and horizontally, as it did not 'look square'.

error_description: A student is unable to see beyond an imperfect physical model of a mathematical space, erroneously assigning the physical properties of the model to the mathematical space itself.
example: Jim wrote that there were no real symmetries on the hyperbolic plane because the crocheted model shape was always changing, wobbly, and stretchy.
authors: Barbara S. Edwards, Ed Dubinsky, Michael A. McDonald
